notes.note: Hale reads Actium as a decisive battle that fixed the Empire's future and let Octavian become Augustus. This is the author's judgment of its consequences, not a claim about forces or command.
notes.quotation: Actium was one of the decisive battles of the world—the event that fixed the destinies of the Roman Empire for centuries to come

drafts.subject: chr:entity:augustus

qualifierQuotations.text: Antony was now his only remaining rival.

drafts.quotation: Octavian, the dictator of the West, had expelled Lepidus from the African provinces that had been assigned to him as his territory. Antony was now his only remaining rival.
drafts.rationale: The author calls the future emperor Octavian, which maps to Augustus per the inquiry guidance. 'Antony' is Mark Antony, named with Octavian and Lepidus among the triumvirs earlier in the passage. 'His only remaining rival' refers back to Octavian.
drafts.relevance: Through the military lens, the rivalry between the two commanders is the political and strategic basis of the civil war that ended at Actium.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:mark-antony
drafts.quotation: Antony was preparing to carry the war into Italy, and assembled on the western shores of Greece an army made up of the Roman legions of the eastern provinces and large contingents of Oriental allies
drafts.rationale: Hale says Antony himself assembled the army from eastern legions and Oriental allies on the western Greek coast, which shows his supreme authority over it. 'Antony' is Mark Antony. The army is mapped to his land army at Actium, which is the same force by the later campaign.
drafts.relevance: Shows who held authority over the land force Antony gathered before the Actium campaign, through the military lens.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:mark-antony

drafts.rationale: The fleet is called 'Antony's war fleet' and is strengthened by Phoenician and Egyptian squadrons, which shows his authority over it. It is mapped to his fleet at Actium. The passage says nothing about who commanded it in action.
drafts.relevance: Shows Antony's formal authority over the fleet and its composition before the battle, through the military lens.

notes.note: Hale reads the civil war as a contest between Eastern and Western influences over the Roman world, as well as between two rulers.
notes.quotation: whether Eastern or Western influences were to predominate in shaping its destinies

drafts.subject: chr:entity:marcus-vipsanius-agrippa
drafts.quotation: his admiral was the celebrated Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa
drafts.rationale: The passage calls Agrippa Octavian's admiral over the Western fleet that is to meet Antony's. 'Admiral' is the author's gloss and is not used as a role. I identified him by his full name, Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa.
drafts.relevance: Names the officer who directed Octavian's fleet, which the lens asks about when separating authority from command.
ambiguities: The passage describes the fleet before the campaign and shows no action, so command in the battle itself is inferred from 'his admiral'.

drafts.subject: chr:entity:augustus
drafts.quotation: His fleet crowded the ports of Tarentum (Taranto) and Brundusium (Brindisi)
drafts.rationale: The author calls it 'his fleet', meaning Octavian's, and the author names Octavian throughout, so I mapped him to Augustus. The passage ties the fleet to Octavian's decision to carry the war to Greece.
drafts.relevance: Shows Octavian's formal ownership of the Western fleet, separate from the admiral who led it.

notes.note: Contrast in manpower: Antony's crews are hastily recruited landsmen, Octavian's are experienced sailors, many of them Liburnians.
notes.quotation: Antony's fleet was largely manned by hastily recruited landsmen, Octavian had crews made up of experienced sailors

notes.note: Composition of the two fleets: Octavian's mostly triremes, smaller than the huge quinqueremes and larger ships reported in Antony's fleet.
notes.quotation: The ships of the Western Empire were mostly triremes

notes.note: Hale's own judgment of what Antony should have done in reply to Agrippa's raid: put to sea, force a pitched battle, and decide who held the command of the sea. It is the author's view, not narrative fact.
notes.quotation: Antony ought to have replied to this challenge by putting to sea with his combined fleet

notes.note: Hale explains Antony's passivity by his character: once energetic, now indolent and irresolute, and so surrendering the initiative at sea to the other side.
notes.quotation: But Cæsar's old lieutenant, once as energetic and enterprising a soldier as his master, had now become indolent and irresolute.

notes.note: Hale's figure for the size of Antony's fleet: some five hundred ships, among them large merchantmen hastily fitted for war. This is one author's number, not a reconciled count.
notes.quotation: There were some five hundred in all, including, however, a number of large merchantmen hastily fitted for war service.

notes.note: Hale's own judgment that the timber barricades slowed Antony's ships and made turning harder, so they increased the very danger of ramming they were meant to avert.
notes.quotation: But the invention had the drawback of diminishing the speed of the ship, and making quick turning more difficult, and thus it increased the very danger it was intended to avert.

notes.note: The author explains the camp's entrenchments and the earthwork-protected road to the fleet station as an instance of Roman habit in campaigning, a logistics and field-works detail for Octavian's land force.
notes.quotation: it was the custom of the Romans to make as much use of pick and spade as of sword and spear in their campaigns

notes.note: Hale describes the mixed eastern composition of Antony's moored fleet: Phoenician and Egyptian ships with gaudy fittings. He sets this beside Cleopatra's state galley, giving a picture of the force's make-up without any command or authority claim.
notes.quotation: Many of the ships of Phœnicia and Egypt displayed an Eastern profusion of colour in their painted upper works, their gilded bows, and their bright flags and streamers.

unresolvedMentions.note: The gulf where Antony's fleet lay moored; it is not in the in-scope entity list.

notes.note: Hale gives the make-up of Antony's land army at Actium: Roman legions under veterans of Caesar's wars, Egyptian battalions, and levies of the tributary Eastern kings. No numbers are given.
notes.quotation: It was a mixed gathering of many nations—Roman legions commanded by veterans of the wars of Cæsar; Egyptian battalions in the quaint war dress we see on the painted walls of tombs by the Nile, and the semi-barbarous levies of the tributary kings of Eastern Asia.

notes.note: Hale attributes the discontent among Antony's Roman officers and men to Antony's deference to Cleopatra, and the Eastern kings' wavering to the chance of a better deal with Octavian. This is the author's reading of the morale of Antony's side.
notes.quotation: Not a few of the Romans were chafing at their leader's subservience to a "Barbarian" queen.

drafts.quotation: But for the commanders, Octavian and his able lieutenant, there was nothing to regret.
drafts.rationale: The passage calls Octavian (mapped to Augustus) a commander and gives him a lieutenant. The lieutenant is not named here; I identify him as Agrippa from the surrounding sections, which describe Agrippa directing Octavian's fleet.
drafts.relevance: Shows through the military lens that Hale presents Agrippa as Octavian's subordinate commander in the victorious Western fleet at Actium.
ambiguities: The passage does not name the lieutenant; the identification with Agrippa rests on the surrounding context.

notes.note: Hale reads Actium as a decisive contest between East and West that left Octavian well placed to become master of the Roman world.
notes.quotation: The battle had once more decided the issue between East and West

notes.note: The victorious rank and file are said to have been disappointed because Cleopatra's treasure, which they had hoped to take as a prize, left with the Egyptian fleet.
notes.quotation: They had hoped to secure as a prize the treasures of Cleopatra, but these had been spirited away on the Egyptian fleet.
